summary: Explains why the IESG considered granting a variance to the standards process rules so the revised BGP-4 specification can refer normatively to RFC 2385, the TCP MD5 signature option. Usually a document may only depend on others at the same or a higher maturity level. RFC 2385 itself stays at Proposed Standard. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally you can only lean on friends of equal rank. This memo explains why an exception is made so BGP can rely on a lower-ranked protection method.

questions: tcp md5 signature option standards variance
why does bgp use tcp md5
subtitle: Why BGP-4 can normatively reference a weaker security standard than usual.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 needed to normatively reference RFC 2385 (TCP MD5 Signature), but IETF rules say a standard document can only depend on other standards at the same or higher maturity level. RFC 2385 is only Proposed Standard, while BGP-4 was being made Draft Standard.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) evaluated whether RFC 2385 was fit for BGP use despite being at a lower maturity level. They found it has cryptographic weaknesses but remains adequate for BGP's specific deployment environment because BGP connections are short-lived, mostly one hop, and confined to trusted networks.
tldr.outcome: The IESG granted a variance allowing BGP-4 to depend on RFC 2385 as a normative reference, acknowledging that better security mechanisms exist but are not worth deploying in BGP's particular operational context.

today: RFC 4278 is Informational. The variance it describes remains in place: BGP-4 normatively references RFC 2385 at Proposed Standard, and the two protocols continue to be used together in Internet routing.

sections.title: The Standards Maturity Problem
sections.content:
The IETF Standards Process (RFC 2026) has a rule: all normative references in a document must be to standards at the same or higher maturity level. The three main levels are Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and Internet Standard. BGP-4 (RFC 4271) needed to normatively reference RFC 2385, the TCP MD5 Signature Option, which provides authentication for BGP connections.

However, RFC 2385 is only at Proposed Standard level, while BGP-4 was being published as Draft Standard. This created a maturity mismatch. RFC 2026 section 9.1 allows the IESG to grant a variance to this rule in exceptional cases. This memo explains why the IESG decided to grant such a variance for BGP-4 and RFC 2385.
sections.plainLanguage: Standards have levels of officiality. A rule cannot usually use a lower-level rule as a foundation. But for BGP, the security bosses made an exception.

sections.title: Why TCP MD5 Is Not Ideal
sections.content:
RFC 2385 describes a Message Authentication Code (MAC) based on a keyed hash function using MD5. When it was written in 1998, this was considered reasonable, but cryptanalysis has since shown the construct to be weaker than originally believed. More problematically, MD5 itself has shown signs of weakness. The IETF community has adopted HMAC (RFC 2104) as the standard MAC because it has provable security properties.

Beyond cryptography, RFC 2385 has operational weaknesses: it includes no key management technique, leaving implementations to rely on passwords as shared secrets (which RFC 3562 warns against). The option lacks a type code or version number, and systems using it cannot accept certain valid TCP resets.

The IESG concluded that RFC 2385 is not suitable for advancement to Draft Standard and would not recommend it for uses outside of BGP. However, the document noted that it is widely deployed in BGP despite these limitations.
sections.plainLanguage: The way TCP MD5 hides data has been cracked a little bit, and the math it uses (MD5) is getting weaker. Cryptography experts would use something stronger for most things.

sections.title: Why BGP Is Different
sections.content:
BGP connections are fundamentally different from most network interactions. Most external BGP (eBGP) links are direct point-to-point connections, just one hop. Even internal BGP (iBGP) sessions are usually only between routers within a single autonomous system, using links that carry only router-to-router traffic, not general-purpose computers.

BGP peering associations are long-lived and static, not dynamic and short-lived like typical web connections. These characteristics limit the attack surface: potential TCP hijacking attacks are harder when the connection is short-lived, runs over a single hop where layer-1 and layer-2 security matter, and only involves routers (which are harder for attackers to use as tools).

However, BGP remains vulnerable to one class of attack that no transmission security mechanism can prevent: false route advertisements from autonomous systems more than one hop away. That threat would require path-validation schemes like S-BGP, not just message authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP routers talk to neighbors very close by, on secure networks, and keep the same connections for years. In that environment, even a weak lock is pretty safe.

sections.title: Alternative Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
Other possible mechanisms for securing BGP exist: IPsec (RFC 2401) and TLS (RFC 2246) could both provide stronger security than TCP MD5. However, these alternatives were rarely or never used in BGP deployments at the time this RFC was written.

The IESG considered whether advancing BGP-4 would be better served by requiring one of these stronger mechanisms. However, they concluded that the marginal security benefit would not justify the transition effort in BGP's particular deployment context. Operators had years of operational experience with TCP MD5 and deployed it widely; asking them to switch to IPsec or TLS would impose significant operational burden for limited gain.

The IESG stated that they would prefer to wait for a security mechanism tailored specifically to BGP's threat environment rather than force deployment of general-purpose mechanisms that do not match BGP's actual risk profile.
sections.plainLanguage: Stronger lock types exist, but putting in a strong lock everywhere would cost a lot more work than the extra safety is worth in routers' safe networks.
